raw_case_text:
The patient was an 88-year-old man of Mediterranean descent, with a history of cirrhosis and underlying HBV infection. At the time of presentation in the clinic, he complained of generalized weakness and fatigue over the last month. Physical examination revealed icterus of the skin and sclera, as well as abdominal distention, owing to the presence of ascitic fluid without any detectable hepatosplenomegaly.
The peripheral blood count showed macrocytic anemia (Hb: 11,6 g / dL, MCV: 108,0 fL), thrombocytopenia (PLT: 113 x 103/ muL) and normal WBC count and differential. In particular, the exact values were as follows: WBC: 4,0 x 103/ muL, Neut.: 72%, Lymph.: 18%, Mono.: 9,0%, Eosino.: 1,0%, RBC: 3,09 x 106/ muL, Hb: 11,6 g / dL, MCV: 108,0 fL, MCH: 37,6 pg, and PLT: 113 x 103/ muL. His serum profile provided the following results: Gluc: 105,0 mg / dl, UREA: 32,0 mg / dL, CREAT: 0,88 mg / dL, SGOT: 223,0 U / L, SGPT: 155 U / L, T-Bil.: 7,0 mg / dL, Bl-Bil.: 3,0 mg / dL, gamma-GTP: 50 U / L, ALP: 165 U / L, LDH: 241 U / L, Prot: 7,4 g / dL, Alb: 2,1 g / dL, CK: 183 U / L. The biochemical examination of the collected peritoneal fluid revealed: Gluc 111 mg / dL, Prot: 2,2 g / dL, Alb: 0,65 g / dL, LDH: 1590 U / L, Chol: 7,0 mg / dL, and Trigl: 16 mg / dL.
Abdominal Ultrasound-Sonography (US) demonstrated liver cirrhosis and massive ascites. Computed-Tomography (CT), which was carried out later confirmed the ascites, although with no visible peritoneal implants. Furthermore, no pathological lymphadenopathy was detected by the obtained CT-scans.
Paracentesis was performed, yielding a large amount (800 ml) of ascitic fluid that was subsequently sent for cytological evaluation. After centrifugation of the sample, the sediment was used for ThinPrep preparation as well as for routine preparation, with direct smearing stained with both Pap and Giemsa. The remaining sediment was used for cell block preparation, using the plasma-thrombin method and standard H and E staining.
The Thin Prep material consisted of abundant large-sized malignant cells, with a moderate amount of basophilic cytoplasm, which were arranged singly. Most of them had a single nucleus, but occasionally, bi-nucleated or multinucleated cells were also seen. The nucleus had coarse chromatin pattern, irregular nuclear outlines, and a single or multiple prominent nucleoli. A high mitotic activity, with abnormal mitoses was present, and a large number of apoptotic bodies as well as nuclear debris were additionally seen [Figures 1a and 1b].
The immunophenotypic profile of the tumor was determined by standard immunoperoxidase methods using paraffin sections from cell block material. The primary antibodies used were: AE1 / AE3, EMA, Vimentin, Melan A, MPO, Fascin, Perforin, Bcl-6, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD15, CD20, CD30, CD34, CD43, CD45 (LCA), CD45RO, and CD138 antigens. In addition, anaplastic lymphoma kinase 1 (ALK-1) protein, TIA-1, LMP-1, and HHV-8 (Latent Nuclear Antigen-1; LANA-1) were also investigated. Antigen retrieval was performed using ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA)-based solution (CC1). The primary antibody, secondary antibody, and avidin-enzyme conjugate were then visualized using the precipitating enzyme diaminobenzidine (DAB). The detailed immunocytochemical list of the antibodies used in our case is depicted in Table 1.
A possible Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection was excluded using the EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) in situ hybridization test in cell block material. On the contrary, the infection with he Hepatitis B virus was further confirmed with the identification of the HBV-DNA. Moreover, sediment from the ascitic fluid was examined using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method to detect any clonal rearrangement of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene (IgH). Moreover, we checked for gene rearrangement in the T-cell receptor. In particular, and in more detail, the methods used are described below and the obtained results are shown in the attached figures.
Molecular analysis was performed using the IdentiClone IgH Gene Clonality Assay kit (CE-IVD, InVivoScribe Technologies, USA). The DNA was extracted and amplified by primers that target the conserved framework of the variable (V) regions, the conserved joining (J) regions, as well as the diversity and joining regions, according to the manufacturer's instructions. The DNA quality was tested by the Specimen Control Size Ladder Mix, which contains multiple oligonucleotides targeting the housekeeping genes [supplied with the Kit, Figure 3].
The presence or absence of clonal T-cell Receptor Gamma chain gene rearrangements was evaluated using the IdentiClone TCRG Gene Clonality Assay (CE-IVD, InVivoScribe Technologies, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions, as mentioned earlier.
The PCR products were analyzed in agarose gel electrophoresis, followed by non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE), in the presence of positive (clonal) and negative (polyclonal) controls [Figures 4-6].
A bone-marrow aspirate showed no evidence of lymphoma. The serological investigation revealed the following results: HbsAg: (+), Anti-Hbc: IgG(+), Anti-Hbe: (-), HbeAg: (+), Anti-Hbs: (-), Anti-HCV: (-), and Anti-HIV: (-).
The final diagnosis that was based on both cytological and immunocytochemical findings, in conjunction with the appropriate molecular workup, was indicative of primary effusion lymphoma with aberrant T-cell expression. The patient unfortunately died one week after the final diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 88-year-old man of Mediterranean descent with hepatitis B virus-related cirrhosis presented with a 1-month history of generalized weakness, fatigue, jaundice, and progressive abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding month, the patient experienced progressively worsening generalized weakness, fatigue, cutaneous and scleral icterus, and abdominal distension due to massive ascites.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of liver cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1-month generalized weakness, fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal distension.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous and scleral icterus and marked abdominal distension with massive ascites without palpable hepatosplenomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, MCV 108.0 fL, MCH 37.6 pg, RBC 3.09 x 10^6/µL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 113 x 10^3/µL), and normal WBC (4.0 x 10^3/µL; 72% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes, 9% monocytes, 1% eosinophils). Serum biochemistry showed glucose 105.0 mg/dL, urea 32.0 mg/dL, creatinine 0.88 mg/dL, AST (SGOT) 223.0 U/L, ALT (SGPT) 155 U/L, total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, GGT 50 U/L, ALP 165 U/L, LDH 241 U/L, total protein 7.4 g/dL, albumin 2.1 g/dL, and CK 183 U/L. Viral serologies were positive for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgG, HBeAg, and serum HBV DNA, and negative for anti-HBs, anti-HBe, anti-HCV, and anti-HIV. Ascitic fluid biochemistry (800 mL paracentesis) showed glucose 111 mg/dL, protein 2.2 g/dL, albumin 0.65 g/dL, markedly elevated LDH 1,590 U/L, cholesterol 7.0 mg/dL, and triglycerides 16 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed cirrhosis and massive ascites.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT confirmed liver cirrhosis and massive ascites without peritoneal implants or pathological lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow aspirate was negative for lymphoma. Ascitic fluid ThinPrep cytology and cell-block immunocytochemistry demonstrated large pleomorphic malignant lymphoid cells with basophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and brisk atypical mitoses positive for HHV-8 (LANA-1), CD45, CD30, EMA, CD138, Perforin, and aberrant T-cell markers (CD3/CD4/CD5/CD43/CD45RO) and negative for EBER ISH and B-cell surface markers. IdentiClone PCR clonality assays on ascitic cell DNA confirmed clonal rearrangements of both the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) and T-cell receptor gamma (TCRG) genes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HHV-8-positive, EBV-negative peritoneal primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) with aberrant T-cell antigen expression and dual IgH/TCRG gene rearrangements in an HIV-negative 88-year-old Mediterranean man with HBeAg-positive HBV cirrhosis. Confirmed by ascitic fluid cytology, HHV-8 LANA-1 immunocytochemistry, and molecular PCR clonality studies, without solid nodal or bone marrow involvement. The patient deteriorated rapidly and died 1 week after final diagnosis.
